title: Paired Tissue and Plasma Comprehensive Genomic Profiling in Advanced Solid Tumors: A Retrospective Study from India.
authors: Bahl A, Rohatgi N, Karanth SS et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Tissue and plasma comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP) sample different compartments and may yield nonoverlapping clinically relevant findings. We assessed the added patient-level yield of paired testing in a pan-cancer cohort from India.
METHODS: This retrospective, single-institution study included patients with stage IV solid tumors who underwent paired tissue and plasma CGP between November 2022 and October 2024. The primary endpoint was detection in a patient of an OncoKB Level 1 or Level 2 or R1 alteration, high tumor mutational burden, or microsatellite instability. Molecularly informed therapy and laboratory turnaround time were assessed descriptively.
RESULTS: Of 158 patients, 123 matched evaluable pairs were analyzed. Either modality detected a clinically relevant finding in 46 of 123 patients (37.4%; 95% confidence interval, 29.4-46.2%): tissue CGP in 33 (26.8%), plasma CGP in 35 (28.5%), both in 22 (17.9%), tissue only in 11 (8.9%) and plasma only in 13 (10.6%). This complementarity remained bidirectional across exploratory analyses, including a subgroup that excluded non-small cell lung cancer (33.0%), all 139 technically successful pairs (33.8%), all 158 paired sample sets (32.3%), and even when the endpoint was restricted to OncoKB alterations (22.0%). Among 91 patients with therapy-alignment data, 25 (27.5%) received molecularly informed therapy. Median laboratory turnaround time was 7 days for plasma and 13 days for tissue CGP.
CONCLUSIONS: Tissue and plasma CGP were complementary rather than interchangeable in this selected cohort: either modality alone would have missed clinically relevant findings. Whether this improves outcomes is untested; prospective studies linking testing strategy to treatment delivery and survival are needed.

title: MRD-Guided Postoperative Surveillance and Adaptive Treatment for Resectable Lung Cancer
interventions: Adaptive therapy of de-escalation and escalation based on MRD testing and pathological response
summary: This study is a prospective single-arm clinical trial targeting patients with stage IB-IIIA non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who have received neoadjuvant immunotherapy. The primary objective is to evaluate whether a personalized follow-up and adjuvant treatment strategy-based on the combination of ctDNA-based minimal residual disease (MRD) testing and pathological response-can effectively improve the 2-year postoperative recurrence-free survival (RFS). The study will enroll 100 patients scheduled for radical surgery who have undergone neoadjuvant immunotherapy (in combination with platinum-based chemotherapy). Patients will receive individualized follow-up and adjuvant therapy based on dynamic changes in ctDNA at various preoperative and postoperative timepoints, as well as pathological response. Adjuvant therapy will be recommended if patients do not achieve pathological complete response (pCR) after surgery, or if ctDNA testing is positive after neoadjuvant therapy or post-surgery. Only patients who achieve pCR and have negative ctDNA at both specified timepoints will forgo adjuvant therapy; these patients will undergo blood sampling at each routine follow-up, with adjuvant therapy initiated upon ctDNA seroconversion to positive. The primary endpoint is 2-year RFS after surgery; secondary endpoints include overall survival (OS) and the diagnostic rate of recurrence/metastasis based on ctDNA-MRD testing. This project aims to explore the refinement of adaptive treatment strategies in the neoadjuvant immunotherapy lung cancer population, with the ultimate goal of improving overall therapeutic efficacy and establishing a standardized, integrated postoperative management system suitable for lung cancer patients.

title: A Digital Twin Framework for Per-Fraction Prediction of Normal Tissue Toxicity in Radiotherapy of Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
authors: Sud A, Huang J, Hart GR et al.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), often delivered in 3-5 fractions, is a highly effective treatment strategy for early-stage non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) in medically inoperable patients. Biology-guided radiotherapy (BGRT), a PET-guided SBRT, enables acquisition of patient-specific metabolic, anatomical, and dose information at each fraction. While prior models have focused on static, population-level prediction of radiation-induced toxicity, there remains a lack of approaches to characterize how normal tissue response evolves longitudinally within individual patients over the course of radiation treatment. We therefore hypothesize that AI-based models can quantify temporal toxicity patterns in such longitudinal data, allowing clinicians to balance tumor control against normal tissue complications to guide individualized treatment planning. Methods: In this proof-of-concept study, we developed COMPASS (COMprehensive Personalized Assessment System), a digital twin framework that generates per-fraction risk estimates that could inform future adaptive decision-making in NSCLC. With Yale Institutional Review Board approval, eight patients with NSCLC who underwent BGRT were retrospectively included in this study. A total of 99 organ-fraction observations, spanning 24 patient-organ longitudinal trajectories across three organs-at-risk (spinal cord, heart, and esophagus), were used to train a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) autoencoder to learn latent temporal representations, which were subsequently characterized using logistic regression to assess for CTCAE ≥ 1 toxicity. Results: In a leave-one-out patient evaluation, COMPASS achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.90, with 80% sensitivity and 78.6% specificity in predicting normal tissue toxicity at the patient-organ trajectory level on a fractional basis. Conclusions: These findings support the feasibility of AI-driven digital twins for per-fraction toxicity monitoring, offering a step toward personalized radiotherapy for NSCLC patients.

title: Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Patients with Brain Metastases and Limited Access to Systemic Therapy.
authors: Trikhirhisthit K, Berpan A, Neesanun S
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: We aimed to identify prognostic factors associated with overall survival in patients with brain metastases from non-small cell lung cancer (BM-NSCLC) who had limited access to systemic therapy.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 83 patients with BM-NSCLC. Data collected included age, sex, performance status, histology, neurologic symptoms, extracranial metastasis (ECM), and receipt of whole-brain radiotherapy (WBRT) and systemic treatment. Associations between these factors and time to death were assessed using Cox proportional hazards regression analysis.
RESULTS: The mean age of the patients was 63.1±8.9 years. Approximately 30% of patients had ECM, whereas 14% received systemic treatment. Three-quarters of the cohort underwent WBRT. The median survival time was 2.7 months [95% confidence interval (CI): 2.2-4.1 months]. The 6-month and 1-year survival probabilities were 26.5% (95% CI: 17.6%-36.3%) and 9.6% (95% CI: 4.5%-17.1%), respectively. Multivariable analysis demonstrated that ECM was significantly associated with an increased risk of death [adjusted hazard ratio (aHR): 4.22, 95% CI: 1.27-14.0, P = 0.019, for newly diagnosed lung cancer; aHR: 6.33, 95% CI: 1.62-24.79, P = 0.008, for controlled primary lung cancer with ECM; and aHR: 11.32, 95% CI: 2.89-56.1, P = 0.003, for uncontrolled primary lung cancer and ECM]. Receipt of systemic treatment was significantly associated with a lower risk of death (aHR: 0.39, 95% CI: 0.18-0.80, P = 0.011). WBRT was not significantly associated with improved survival (aHR: 0.79, 95% CI: 0.43-1.44, P = 0.441).
CONCLUSION: The presence of ECM and the absence of systemic treatment were significantly associated with shorter survival in patients with BM-NSCLC.

title: Prognostic stratification by the ESTRO/EORTC oligometastatic classification and simplified binary approaches in lung cancer patients treated with stereotactic ablative radiotherapy.
authors: Yao D, Zhu XR, Guo JD et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The ESTRO/EORTC classification categorizes oligometastatic disease (OMD) into de-novo, repeat, and induced OMD based on prior disease history and treatment status. However, its prognostic relevance in lung cancer patients treated with stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR) remains incompletely characterized in real-world settings. This study evaluated the ESTRO/EORTC classification and two simplified binary stratification approaches derived from its decision framework.
METHODS: This single-center retrospective study included 648 lung cancer patients with 1-5 metastases treated with SABR between 2015 and 2021. Patients were categorized according to the ESTRO/EORTC classification. Two simplified binary stratification approaches derived from the ESTRO/EORTC decision framework were additionally explored: (1) a history-based approach distinguishing patients with prior polymetastatic disease from those without, and (2) a therapy-dependent progression approach distinguishing oligometastatic progression during active systemic therapy from other OMD states. Survival outcomes were analyzed using Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression, and prognostic discrimination was assessed using Harrell's C-index.
RESULTS: With a median follow-up of 54.5 months, 325 deaths and 552 progression events were observed. Induced OMD was associated with significantly worse outcomes compared with de-novo OMD (OS: 35.7 vs. 68.9 months; PFS: 8.6 vs. 15.5 months; both p < 0.001) and repeat OMD (OS: 35.7 vs. 60.2 months; PFS: 8.6 vs. 14.4 months; both p < 0.001). No significant differences were observed between de-novo and repeat OMD. The therapy-dependent progression stratification approach demonstrated distinct survival separation (median OS 34.4 vs. 86.4 months; PFS 8.4 vs. 16.4 months; both p < 0.001), although the difference in discriminatory performance was modest (C-index 0.596 for OS) compared with the ESTRO/EORTC classification (0.565) and the history-based approach (0.563). Differences in discriminatory performance were modest and not statistically significant after multiple-testing correction and bootstrap resampling.
CONCLUSIONS: The ESTRO/EORTC classification is associated with survival outcomes in lung cancer patients with OMD treated with SABR, with induced OMD conferring the poorest prognosis. Simplified binary stratification approaches derived from this framework may provide a pragmatic and clinically accessible approach for risk stratification. These approaches should be considered complementary to, rather than replacements for, the full ESTRO/EORTC classification. Prospective validation is warranted.

title: MultiCaRe-Thorax: A Curated Benchmark Dataset and Reproducible Labeling Framework for Multi-Label Thoracic Disease Classification in Chest X-Ray Imaging.
authors: Abu Jassar NJ, Almalkawi IT, Al-Hammouri MF et al.
abstract: Chest X-ray (CXR) imaging remains a widely used diagnostic modality for the detection of thoracic diseases, including pneumonia, tuberculosis, pleural effusion, lung cancer and cardiomegaly. Despite the extensive use of CXR examinations in clinical practice, the development of robust multi-label artificial intelligence (AI) systems remains constrained by limitations in dataset availability, annotation consistency and reproducible labeling methodologies. Existing public datasets frequently rely on heterogeneous labeling protocols, limited pathology coverage or annotations that inadequately account for linguistic negation and uncertainty within radiology reports. In this paper, we introduce MultiCaRe-Thorax, a curated thoracic benchmark dataset derived from the publicly available MultiCaRe repository, with a reproducible negation-aware natural language processing (NLP) framework for automated generation of multi-label thoracic disease annotations. Unlike existing CXR benchmarks that are distributed in their pre-curated form, MultiCaRe-Thorax provides a fully reproducible pipeline from raw case reports to curated dataset, establishing a new resource that is both scalable and transparent. Our pipeline performs thoracic case identification, image-report matching, duplicate removal, data cleaning, disease-specific label extraction and quality-control verification to produce a curated cohort comprising 5252 chest radiographs from 3415 unique patients. Sixteen clinically relevant thoracic pathologies were automatically annotated using a dictionary- and pattern-based NLP framework incorporating explicit negation detection and n-gram mining, achieving 95% accuracy against 500 manually reviewed reports (Cohen's κ=0.89). Sixteen clinically relevant thoracic pathologies were automatically annotated using a dictionary- and pattern-based NLP framework incorporating explicit negation detection and n-gram mining, achieving 95% agreement against 500 manually reviewed reports. Five ImageNet-pretrained convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures (ResNet50, DenseNet121, EfficientNetB0, EfficientNetB7 and InceptionV3) with two hybrid ensemble configurations were evaluated under a patient-level data partitioning protocol. Among individual architectures, DenseNet121 attains the best AUC on tuberculosis (0.757) and pleural effusion (0.767) with roughly one-third the parameters of ResNet50, while ResNet50 attains the higher mean AUC across all sixteen pathologies (0.688 vs. 0.682) and on interstitial lung disease (0.769) and lung mass/cancer (0.777); we report this as an accuracy-efficiency trade-off rather than a single best architecture. The DenseNet121-InceptionV3 ensemble achieves the highest reported AUC of 0.821 for lung mass/cancer detection. We report 95% confidence intervals for the evaluated ensemble and remaining backbones and note substantial estimation uncertainty for the rarest classes (e.g., congenital heart disease, n=8 test cases). Grad-CAM visualizations were also employed to provide clinically interpretable explanations of model predictions.

title: Real-World Impact of Mepolizumab in COPD in a US Commercial and Medicare Claims Database.
authors: Panettieri RA, Paczkowski R, Mei H et al.
journal: Int J Chron Obstruct Pulmon Dis
abstract:
PURPOSE: Mepolizumab reduces exacerbations in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and was recently approved in the United States (US) for the add-on maintenance treatment of adult patients with inadequately controlled COPD and an eosinophilic phenotype. Given the limited real-world data on mepolizumab effectiveness in COPD, this study assessed its real-world impact in patients with COPD, prior to US regulatory approval of mepolizumab for COPD.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: Retrospective, longitudinal analysis from the US Komodo Research claims database (January 2016-June 2024). The first observed mepolizumab claim was defined as the index date. All patients were aged ≥40 years on index date, had ≥2 COPD diagnosis claims in the 12 months pre-index (baseline period) or on index date, and required ≥2 pharmacy/medical claims for mepolizumab from index date to end of observation. Patients with ≥2 asthma diagnosis claims or ≥1 diagnosis claim(s) for cystic fibrosis, lung cancer, interstitial lung disease, or α-1 antitrypsin deficiency during the baseline period or on index date were excluded. Outcomes assessed during the 12 months post- versus 12 months pre-mepolizumab initiation included annualized exacerbation rates, oral corticosteroid (OCS) use, and COPD-related healthcare resource utilization (HCRU).
RESULTS: Descriptive analyses included 693 mepolizumab initiators (58% Medicare), while pre-post analyses included 470 patients with 12 months of pre- and post-initiation data. Annualized rate of moderate/severe exacerbations decreased by 41% (P<0.001) post- versus pre-mepolizumab. Relative reductions of 26% and 33% in rates of OCS dispensing and bursts were observed (P<0.001), and relative reductions of 22-37% in COPD-related HCRU including hospitalizations (P=0.038), emergency department visits (P<0.001), and outpatient visits (P<0.001).
CONCLUSION: In this real-world retrospective study of US patients with COPD, initiation of mepolizumab was associated with significant reductions in COPD exacerbations, OCS use and COPD-related HCRU.

title: Thymoma-associated immunodeficiency: a good review.
authors: Capellini C, Sculco E, Milito C
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Provide clinicians with an overview of the latest findings while remaining pragmatic for everyday clinical practice.
RECENT FINDINGS: More than 70 years after its description, new evidence in the etiopathogenesis of this condition is emerging, starting to create a better understanding of this disease, but most remain unknown. Recently, autoantibody against endogenous cytokines were discovered, more precisely IL-23, IL-6, IL-12, type I and II interferons. Furthermore, overall survival of Good's syndrome improved in recent times from 0% at 15 years to a 20-year survival exceeding 60%. Further studies are necessary to amalgamate current evidence incorporating all the cases described nowadays.
SUMMARY: Good's syndrome is a rare Inborn Error of Immunity characterized by the coexistence of thymoma and immunodeficiency, the latter being defined as hypogammaglobulinemia (classical syndrome) or cellular immunity defects (nonclassical syndrome). This disease leads to predisposition to infections, autoimmunity, and malignancies, with a reduction of life expectancy. Good's syndrome management is focused on thymectomy and immunoglobulin replacement therapy. Increased disease awareness, earlier recognition, and prompt initiation of immunoglobulin replacement therapy showed an improvement in patients' survival.

title: Integrative Bioinformatics and Machine Learning Approaches for Biomarker and Pathway Discovery in Malignant Pleural Mesothelioma.
authors: Rohman ML, Biswas S
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Malignant pleural mesothelioma (MPM) is a highly aggressive thoracic cancer with limited treatment options and poor prognosis.
AIMS: This study employed an integrative transcriptomic and computational approach to uncover potential biomarkers for MPM.
METHODS: Gene expression data from the GSE51024 dataset, comprising 41 normal and 55 MPM tumor samples, were preprocessed using the robust multiarray average (RMA) method. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using the Limma package and Wilcoxon rank tests. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) revealed significant gene modules using topological overlap and preservation statistics, followed by functional annotation through Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG pathway analyses.
RESULTS: Hub genes within conserved modules (MM > 0.8) were identified, including ZNF638, RAB18, SOS1, TTC17, RANBP2, FNDC3B, QSER1, CLDN15, PSTPIP1, SEPTIN6, ADAP2, and PVRIG. Survival analysis validated their prognostic relevance using public databases. Furthermore, high classification accuracy was achieved using various machine learning algorithms (SVM, PLDA, XGB, K-NN, and logistic regression), confirming the discriminative potential of the hub genes. The results highlighted several physiologically significant hub genes and pathways associated with cell cycle regulation, immune modulation, and cancer progression.
CONCLUSION: Overall, this exploratory study demonstrated that potential biomarkers in MPM can be effectively identified using an integrative systems biology and machine learning framework. The identified hub genes may support future diagnostic, prognostic, and personalized treatment strategies for patients with MPM.

title: Efficacy and Safety of Lucitanib in Advanced Thymic Carcinoma: A Randomized Phase II Trial.
authors: Fang W, Zhou C, Wang C et al.
abstract: Advanced thymic carcinoma is a rare, aggressive malignancy with limited treatment options after chemotherapy failure. This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (AL3810-202) aimed to evaluate lucitanib, a novel, orally potent tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting VEGFR1‒3, FGFR1‒3, and PDGFRα/β in patients with advanced thymic carcinoma progressing after chemotherapy. Sixty-eight patients were randomized (2:1) to receive 10 mg lucitanib daily (n = 46) or placebo (n = 22). Although this study did not meet its primary endpoint of independent review committee (IRC)-assessed progression-free survival (PFS) (median 5.8 vs. 3.7 months; hazard ratio [HR]: 0.60; p = 0.1050), the prespecified log-rank test may have underestimated the treatment effect due to an observed non-proportional hazards pattern. Subsequent restricted mean survival time analysis demonstrated a statistically significant PFS benefit (p < 0.05), which was further supported by significantly prolonged investigator-assessed PFS (6.6 vs. 1.9 months; HR: 0.53; p = 0.0306). The most common grade 3 treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) were hypertension (50%), proteinuria (15.2%), and thrombocytopenia (8.7%), with no grade 4/5 events. Considering the totality of the evidence and an acceptable safety profile, lucitanib may confer a meaningful clinical benefit for patients with advanced thymic carcinoma, warranting further investigation.

title: Integrated histopathological, immunohistochemical, and molecular profiling reveals hidden heterogeneity within histologic subtypes of thymoma.
authors: Yeh YC, Hsieh MS, Wang LC et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Thymoma classification is based primarily on histologic features, but the extent to which histologic subtypes reflect underlying molecular diversity remains incompletely defined. Molecular characterization is further complicated by abundant intratumoral lymphocytes, which can reduce tumor purity and limit mutation detection using conventional sequencing approaches.
METHODS: In this study, we performed an integrated histopathological, immunohistochemical, and molecular analysis of 138 surgically resected thymomas. Immunohistochemical staining for ASS1, SATB1, BCL2, and CD20 was evaluated, and high-sensitivity molecular barcoding-based targeted sequencing was used to improve detection of low-variant allele frequency mutations. Epithelial-rich tumors were further evaluated by whole-exome sequencing and TCGA multi-omics analysis.
RESULTS: GTF2I p.L424H mutations were highly prevalent in type A (28/33, 84.8 %) and AB thymomas (50/51, 98.0 %). Among type B thymomas, GTF2I mutations were confined to type B1 tumors (5/16, 31.3 %) and absent in B2 and B3 tumors. GTF2I-mutated B1 thymomas showed low or absent ASS1 expression, resembling type A/AB thymomas, whereas GTF2I-wild-type B1 thymomas showed higher ASS1 expression, similar to other type B thymomas. Whole-exome sequencing revealed molecular heterogeneity among GTF2I-wild-type type A thymomas, with a subset showing high copy number alteration burden and immunophenotypic overlap with type B3 thymomas. TCGA multi-omics analysis further identified a rare GTF2I-mutated type B3 thymoma with type A-like molecular features despite typical B3 morphology.
CONCLUSION: Our findings demonstrate that thymoma subtypes harbor molecular heterogeneity not fully captured by conventional histologic classification. Integrating histopathological, immunohistochemical, and molecular features may provide a more biologically informative framework for thymoma stratification.
